statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2018 survey at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, about 3 in 4 people had used drugs alone at least once in the past week. The reason chosen most often was that using at home is easier and more comfortable; others did not want people to know or felt safer alone, and some wrote that they had no one to use with. The survey could not show whether using alone changes the risk of overdose, but coroners' reports it cites found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose in the province in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.
population: Clients of 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites in all five health regions of British Columbia, Canada, May to August 2018: 414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months (62.6% men; 34.3% not regularly housed; past-week use of opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%), recruited by convenience at the sites
exposure: Using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, from one self-report item (share of the time drugs were used alone, in bands, counted as any against none; alone not defined for respondents)
comparator: Respondents who did not use alone in the past 7 days (100), for the correlates; none for the reasons
outcome: Reasons chosen from a short list (more than one allowed, with free text, from which the authors coded two further reasons), asked only of those who used alone; characteristics associated with using alone; self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months
magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): listed options: convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), safer alone 30 (9.6%); coded by the authors from written answers: no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other reasons that could not be coded 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.

risk_of_bias.note: Convenience sample of site clients with the response rate not reported; 72 of 486 (14.8%) excluded for a missing or prefer-not-to-say answer on using alone; one unvalidated item that did not define alone; reasons limited to pre-worded options (the most chosen joins convenience, comfort and home), with two further reasons coded from written answers and not comparable with the options; correlates from a data-driven model in 306 complete cases without allowance for clustering by site (card sc_papamihali_2020; JBI moderate).

indirectness.note: The overdose part rests on coroners' figures cited second-hand, without definitions; the survey did not record overdoses by occasion.

imprecision.note: 414 respondents give about plus or minus 4 points on the main share.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single survey.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low and is rated as a description of the population sampled (clients of harm reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018); rated down for risk of bias and, for the overdose part, indirectness, giving very low. The main finding, that most clients used alone at least sometimes, is unlikely to be reversed by these biases, but the exact share and the order of reasons depend on who was sampled and how the options were worded. The correlates are associations from a selected model. Status single study.
